related.name: Enterprise pilots with measurable P&L impact

items.text: The "bitter lesson" applies to methods, not products. Real applications still need hand-built business logic, frontends, integrations, and evaluation.
items.title: Application development effort does not vanish

related.name: Enterprise pilots with measurable P&L impact
Developer productivity uplift (METR RCTs)

items.text: A demo that works 90% of the time is a capability, not a product. Executives see quick prototypes and miss the 90% of work needed to finish them.
items.title: Proof-of-concept to product gap

related.name: 50%/80% horizon ratio
METR 80% time horizon

items.text: Accuracy has risen sharply while reliability has moved only a few points. A model that is right 70% of the time but fails unpredictably cannot remove the human from the loop, and reliability fixes are application-specific.
items.title: Capability-reliability gap

related.name: Human interventions on 4–8 hour agent tasks (self-reported)
50%/80% horizon ratio

items.text: An agent making dozens of LLM calls with even a 2% error rate per step becomes useless end to end.
items.title: Compounding unreliability in agents

items.text: People expect AI products to behave like software. Stochastic outputs violate that expectation, and it is unclear whether determinism can be engineered in.
items.title: Users expect software-like determinism

items.text: Current AI products are like PCs before the GUI. Higher-bandwidth interfaces that let users supervise without constant interruption have not been invented.
items.title: Missing interface paradigms

related.name: Enterprise pilots with measurable P&L impact

items.text: General capabilities have to be made useful one domain at a time, which requires deep domain knowledge to find the adoption hurdles (Cursor's code-verification UI is their example).
items.title: Domain-specific product design

items.text: Labs assumed generality exempted them from UX and software engineering, and are rediscovering that both are hard.
items.title: AI companies neglected product engineering

related.name: Price per unit of capability (cheapest METR-hour on OpenRouter)

items.text: Cost, not capability, blocks many applications, especially agentic workflows that call models hundreds of times. Cost also sets accuracy, since retries improve success.
items.title: Cost of inference

items.text: The tasks whose automation would most transform a profession (legal filings, research) have no single correct answer, so they are the hardest to evaluate and improve.
items.title: Judgment tasks resist evaluation

items.text: AI became superhuman at chess because of fast, accurate feedback. Law, medicine, and science have no such verifier, so progress is limited to automatically checkable tasks.
items.title: No verifiers in open domains

items.text: AI reasoning in medicine is limited by the medical knowledge that exists, the same limit humans face.
items.title: Real-world knowledge caps reasoning

items.text: Systems that excel in narrow demos go off the rails in open-ended settings.
items.title: Brittleness outside closed domains

items.text: In their shadow evaluations, frontier agents given real research questions lacked judgment, creativity, and the ability to backtrack or respond to feedback.
items.title: Agents lack judgment for open-ended work

items.text: Agent-built software sacrifices quality, maintainability, and security, and successes often rest on human-built test suites, thousands of lines of prompt, or memorized training data.
items.title: Non-functional requirements go unmet

related.name: Developer productivity uplift (METR RCTs)
50%/80% horizon ratio

items.text: Benchmarks overweight what models are good at, miss contextual reasoning, and encourage agents that score well without being useful. Vendor claims cannot be independently checked.
items.title: Benchmarks lack construct validity

related.name: Developer productivity uplift (METR RCTs)

items.text: Whether a system can automate a job is only knowable after diffusion, because no lab environment captures the world's complexity.
items.title: Real-world messiness cannot be simulated

related.name: Share of work hours assisted by generative AI
US firms using AI (Census BTOS)

items.text: Instant availability to hundreds of millions says nothing about how many people use a capability, for how long, or for what.
items.title: Deployment is not diffusion

related.name: Share of work hours assisted by generative AI
Augmentation vs automation share (Anthropic Economic Index)

items.text: Most users use generative AI infrequently. Nearly a year after release, under 1% of ChatGPT users touched thinking models on a given day.
items.title: Low intensity of use

related.name: Share of work hours assisted by generative AI

items.text: Taking advantage of AI requires continual learning of new workflows and topics. The curve is steep and time-consuming, and it moves at human speed.
items.title: Human learning curves

related.name: US firms using AI (Census BTOS)
US businesses paying for AI (Ramp AI Index)

items.text: The hard part of adoption is users adapting their workflows, which cannot even start in the first months after a launch.
items.title: Workflow and habit change

items.text: Because deployment is instant, people constantly face adoption choices, and the vast majority of the time they decline, for rational and irrational reasons.
items.title: Most adoption decisions are "no."

related.name: Human interventions on 4–8 hour agent tasks (self-reported)

items.text: Agentic work requires constant human supervision, which is time-consuming and mentally exhausting, so realized productivity lags.
items.title: Cost of supervising agents

items.text: Using AI for tasks one has not mastered erodes skill and control, so responsible users limit offloading. Vendor-specific skills replace unaided ones.
items.title: Skill erosion and the dependence spiral

items.text: Past waves of no-code failed because the barrier is not syntax but the judgment and accountability needed to make good decisions.
items.title: Skilled judgment gates "democratization."

items.text: Checking whether an agent actually succeeded at an open-ended task takes deep expertise and time, and long logs cannot be fully reviewed.
items.title: Verification needs domain expertise

items.text: Useful assistants need access to sensitive personal and organizational data, which triggers outcry and regulatory limits on data sharing.
items.title: Privacy resistance

related.name: US firms using AI (Census BTOS)
Share of work hours assisted by generative AI

items.text: For past general-purpose technologies this stage took decades. It has barely begun even in software engineering.
items.title: Organizational change is slower than individual change

related.name: Enterprise pilots with measurable P&L impact
Developer productivity uplift (METR RCTs)

items.text: Like electrification, benefits only arrive once work is reorganized: new layouts, processes, hiring, and training. The restructuring is discovered by experimentation, not designed in advance.
items.title: Drop-in replacement fails

items.text: Much of what organizations know is unwritten and not in training data. It has to be made available to models gradually through adoption, sector by sector.
items.title: Tacit organizational knowledge

items.text: Models must be wired into the many systems organizations already run, a downstream task no model release solves. Enterprise data is locked in Salesforce, Workday, and SAP.
items.title: Integration into existing systems

items.text: Unambiguously saying what is wanted is a large share of the work. Brooks's "essential complexity" of specification is untouched by AI.
items.title: Task specification is human labor

items.text: Understanding requirements and taking accountability for what ships remain human. Once a decision is delegable it stops being a competitive advantage, so human judgment migrates upward.
items.title: The "decide" and "deliver" layers do not compress

items.text: Organizations grant AI access to consequential decisions only after it proves reliable in less critical contexts.
items.title: Staged trust

related.name: Human interventions on 4–8 hour agent tasks (self-reported)
Developer productivity uplift (METR RCTs)

items.text: Requiring approval of every action mostly destroys the value of automation, so it degrades into rubber-stamping or is outcompeted.
items.title: Human-in-the-loop erodes benefits

items.text: Structural change requires solving coordination problems or reforming institutions, which is far less predictable than user behavior (air traffic control is their example).
items.title: Collective action and sclerotic institutions

related.name: US total factor productivity, private nonfarm business

items.text: Diffusion depends on public goods the private sector underprovides: AI literacy, workforce training, digitization, open data.
items.title: Underinvestment in complements

related.name: US firms using AI (Census BTOS)

items.text: Following Jeffrey Ding, countries differ enormously in their ability to spread innovations through the economy, and this, not who reaches a milestone first, sets economic outcomes.
items.title: National diffusion capacity

items.text: Transforming workplaces requires forward-deployed engineers and consulting partnerships, labor-intensive work outside the product.
items.title: Bespoke deployment

items.text: Embedded "digital workers" create extreme lock-in and target labor budgets, so enterprises resist, withhold data for training, and demand portability.
items.title: Enterprise resistance to lock-in

related.name: Entry-level employment shortfall in AI-exposed occupations
Recent-graduate unemployment rate (NY Fed)

items.text: Automating entry-level tasks removes the experiences through which juniors build expertise, a cost that emerges only over time.
items.title: Deskilling breaks the talent pipeline

related.name: US labour productivity, year on year

items.text: Impact arrives through countless mundane process and policy tweaks, not a single leap.
items.title: Millions of small adaptations

items.text: FDA, EU AI Act, and sector rules make deployment slow by design, and regulation often outright prohibits current AI use in productive settings.
items.title: Regulation in high-consequence domains

items.text: Unclear application of liability law deters adoption. Clear rules (FAA drone rules in 2016) spur it.
items.title: Liability uncertainty

items.text: Malpractice liability, professional codes, and device regulation keep doctors from delegating decisions to chatbots.
items.title: Professional guardrails

items.text: Rules insensitive to experimentation reify business models and organizational forms prematurely, and binary automated/not-automated rules discourage new oversight designs.
items.title: Regulation that freezes categories

items.text: Regulation blind to the developer/deployer split saddles general-purpose model makers with context-specific obligations.
items.title: Misplaced burdens on model developers

items.text: UPL rules and their state-by-state vagueness deter new entrants, and bar associations cite model unreliability as grounds for caution.
items.title: Unauthorized practice of law

items.text: Restrictions on who can own or share fees with law firms block outside capital and scaled business models.
items.title: Law firm ownership rules

items.text: Lawyers and commerce groups lobby to narrow regulatory sandboxes despite scant evidence of harm.
items.title: Incumbent resistance to reform

items.text: The speed of human judges, lawyers, and clients caps how fast legal processes can move. Adding judges is politically fraught, and Article III likely requires human judges.
items.title: Human adjudication time

items.text: Flooded courts respond by tightening doctrines to keep litigants out or by banning AI, counteracting the gains.
items.title: Courts may restrict access

items.text: Platform policies require developer accounts, 2FA dialogs that block synthetic input, and a human pressing publish.
items.title: Policy-mandated human steps

items.text: Veto points and proceduralism hobble governments' ability to deploy AI, coordinate resilience, or even provide services they could.
items.title: State capacity sclerosis

items.text: Self-driving cars took 15+ years to deploy and now face bans because policymakers failed to prepare. Public anxiety and backlash from rushed deployments are headwinds.
items.title: Policy backlash

items.text: Treatments need trials with thousands of people over 10 to 15 years. Progress needs data from real experiments that faster AI cannot speed up, and society will not let AI run large-scale experiments on people.
items.title: Clinical trials and real-world experiments

items.text: Where mistakes are expensive and the world cannot be simulated (driving), safety throttles each iteration of the improvement loop.
items.title: Costly, unsimulable errors

items.text: In an already technological, regulated world, the workflow parts AI improves were optimized by earlier waves. The true bottlenecks resist for external reasons.
items.title: AI targets non-bottleneck steps

items.text: Jobs bundle inspection, loading, paperwork, and negotiation with the "core" task. Bio-harm still depends on materials, equipment, and tacit know-how.
items.title: Physical and social task bundles

items.text: Deployment depends on systems the developer does not control. An app took 45 minutes to build and ten days to pass App Store review.
items.title: Slow external review

related.name: Circular financing scale
Cloud backlog (remaining performance obligations)

items.text: Grid capacity constrains training and inference. Token supply is scarce today. Breakthroughs deploy slowly when supporting infrastructure does not exist yet (steam to electric took 40 years).
items.title: Infrastructure, energy, and compute

items.text: Many tasks resemble long-range weather forecasting, where mathematical limits are already reached. Forecasting and persuasion have high irreducible error.
items.title: Inherent limits on prediction

items.text: Constraints like RL environments or energy only become visible once they bind, and if many hard steps remain, a hundredfold speedup on the AI-amenable parts yields a small overall gain.
items.title: Unrecognized latent bottlenecks and Amdahl's law

items.text: They predict slow diffusion will remain the norm where errors matter, enforced by regulators and by organizations' own caution.
items.title: Safety limits in high-consequence tasks

related.name: Human interventions on 4–8 hour agent tasks (self-reported)
50%/80% horizon ratio

items.text: Poorly controlled AI is bad business. Unrecoverable failures like deleting production data make companies pull back from hasty automation.
items.title: Business incentives against unsupervised deployment

items.text: For now an agent can be only two of the three, which keeps AI a collaboration technology rather than an automation one.
items.title: The general-purpose / high-stakes / automated trilemma

items.text: Removing humans from task boundaries to let AI run end to end reduces oversight, so autonomy is checked by the need to keep systems legible.
items.title: Legibility and control

items.text: Liability law and sector regulation are speed controls society can strengthen deliberately, regardless of capability.
items.title: Society's choice to keep humans accountable

items.text: Prompt injection, data leakage, and agent worms must be solved before assistants get broad access; scaffolds capable enough to test the frontier carry risks that may prevent use.
items.title: Security risks of capable scaffolds

related.name: Price per unit of capability (cheapest METR-hour on OpenRouter)
Consumer surplus from generative AI (willingness to accept)

items.text: Once a task is automated its value collapses and humans move to unautomated tasks, so the AGI goalpost keeps moving.
items.title: Automation devalues the automated task

related.name: Price per unit of capability (cheapest METR-hour on OpenRouter)
Concentration of business AI spend across labs (Ramp, HHI)
Semiconductors' share of stack operating income

items.text: In law and science, competition is so intense that productivity gains fuel escalation rather than societal value.
items.title: Competitive arms races dissipate gains

items.text: Buyers cannot verify the quality of legal work or judgment-heavy AI output even in hindsight, so they rely on prestige and trust, and normal price competition fails.
items.title: Credence goods

items.text: Billable hours reward more hours and more output regardless of outcome, absorbing efficiency gains.
items.title: Input-based incentives

related.name: US total factor productivity, private nonfarm business
US labour productivity, year on year

items.text: AI's uneven sectoral effects mean long-run growth is bottlenecked by wherever it diffuses least.
items.title: Growth is capped by the slowest sector

related.name: Lab recoupment ratio
Public cloud software valuation multiples (Clouded Judgement)
Application layer's share of enterprise generative-AI spend (Menlo)

items.text: Undifferentiated models push inference to marginal cost, outcomes are hard to measure so value pricing stalls, and incumbents own distribution. This limits how far labs can fund diffusion.
items.title: Commodity trap and recoupment

items.text: More apps do not increase usage, capping AI's impact on consumer software.
items.title: Fixed consumer attention

items.text: Media organizations' justified wariness and inability to bargain collectively limit the use of journalistic content.
items.title: Publisher distrust

items.text: Cheap generation of results will not unlock progress because producing findings is not what limits science.
items.title: Production of findings is not the bottleneck

items.text: Attention is finite. As volume explodes, novel work is lost and AI search concentrates attention on already-famous papers.
items.title: Overproduction drowns novel work

items.text: Institutions reward measurable production, making researchers risk-averse and making AI a tool for chasing metrics. Reform is blocked by inertia and Goodhart's law.
items.title: Publish-or-perish incentives

items.text: Most AI-for-science is software work, but fields have not adopted testing, version control, or code review, so leakage and other errors affect hundreds of papers.
items.title: Scientists lack software engineering practice

items.text: Code and data go unshared, reviewers do not check code, retractions are near zero, and there is no incentive to debunk.
items.title: Science does not self-correct

items.text: AI improves predictive accuracy without explanation, like epicycles, so wrong theories can persist and human understanding, which is the point of science, erodes.
items.title: Prediction without understanding

items.text: Adopting AI requires re-litigating validity per field and model type, which no field can do in a couple of years.
items.title: Epistemology change exceeds field capacity

items.text: AI-for-science tools chase headlines rather than real bottlenecks like error detection, and are evaluated on time saved, not on understanding.
items.title: Misdirected tools and funding

items.section: Upstream: why AI cannot simply accelerate its own diffusion
items.text: Limits on AI's power sit in deployment, not in the system's design, so improving the design cannot overcome them.
items.title: External bottlenecks are immune to self-improvement

items.section: Upstream: why AI cannot simply accelerate its own diffusion
items.text: Research herds around fashionable ideas, compute and cost constrain new paradigms, and the industry's culture of open sharing is fading. The AI community may be unusually bad at finding new paradigms.
items.title: Herding, compute, and declining openness in methods research

items.section: Upstream: why AI cannot simply accelerate its own diffusion
items.text: Readily available data is spent, and more data costs ever more in money, licensing, and reputational risk. Continued scaling is a business decision, not a technical given.
items.title: Data exhaustion

items.section: Upstream: why AI cannot simply accelerate its own diffusion
items.text: Every capability increase creates new demand for domain-specific evaluation, which resists automation and absorbs human effort.
items.title: Evaluation does not scale
